coverage.learning_objective: Hold a PM-depth conversation with engineering to sanity-check a proposed solution's feasibility before committing it to a roadmap.

required_facts.statement: Technical feasibility assesses whether a proposed solution can be built with the available technology, skills, and constraints.
A PM supplies the intended user outcome and product constraints while engineering evaluates technical options and limitations.
Ask engineering about implementation constraints, dependencies, technical uncertainty, and the effort needed to achieve the proposed behavior.
Clarify whether an answer identifies a hard constraint, a manageable risk, or a cost-and-scope tradeoff, then adjust the proposal accordingly.

misconceptions.statement: A PM-depth feasibility discussion is not a substitute for engineering’s implementation design.
source_refs: scrum_guide#https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html :: Topic Three: How will the chosen work get done?

teaching_blocks.title: Technical Feasibility Assessment (PM-Depth) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A proposal promises a closing summary before anyone has checked whether the necessary information and constraints permit it. PM-depth feasibility work brings the intended outcome and product boundaries to engineering, while leaving technical options and implementation design with the people responsible for that evaluation.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Technical feasibility assesses whether a proposed solution can be built with the available technology, skills, and constraints. A PM supplies the intended user outcome and product constraints while engineering evaluates technical options and limitations.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Ask engineering about implementation constraints, dependencies, technical uncertainty, and the effort needed to achieve the proposed behavior. Clarify whether an answer identifies a hard constraint, a manageable risk, or a cost-and-scope tradeoff, then adjust the proposal accordingly.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative conversation, explain that owners need to identify unfinished paid orders at closing and describe the intended summary behavior. Ask engineering what data or dependencies are required, what is uncertain, and what effort is needed. If an answer says a required status source is unavailable, clarify whether that is a hard constraint, a manageable risk, or a tradeoff requiring changed scope or cost. A narrower behavior may be possible; a missing essential input may require postponing the proposal. Record the clarified implications and adjust the product proposal accordingly. Do not supply an invented architecture or assume that a PM's confidence replaces engineering's technical evaluation.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the discussion anchored in the outcome the product must support and the constraints it must respect. “Can we build it?” becomes more informative when followed by questions about limitations, uncertainty, dependencies, and effort. Your responsibility in this example is to understand what the answers mean for scope and commitment, not to substitute for implementation design.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A PM-depth feasibility discussion is not a substitute for engineering’s implementation design.

teaching_blocks.title: Sprint Planning (PM/PO Involvement) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team is preparing its next sprint and needs both a clear purpose and feasible selected work. Sprint Planning is collaborative across the Scrum Team. The PM or PO contribution is to clarify product value and scope, not to dictate the Developers' implementation plan.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Sprint Planning creates the upcoming sprint’s plan through collaboration across the Scrum Team. The Product Owner prepares the important backlog items and explains how they map to the Product Goal.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The team establishes a Sprint Goal, while Developers select feasible work using their past performance and upcoming capacity. Prepare a PM/PO briefing with the proposed goal, priority rationale, clear item scope, and answers to value or requirement questions.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative briefing, propose a goal of making unfinished paid orders visible in the closing view. Prepare the important backlog items, explain their priority in relation to the Product Goal, and be ready to answer value and requirement questions. The team establishes the Sprint Goal, while Developers select feasible work using past performance and upcoming capacity. If detail access does not fit, clarify the value or scope implications instead of demanding that every proposed item be selected. Developers also determine how the selected work becomes a working increment; the product briefing does not turn that technical planning into a PM instruction sheet.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Separate preparing candidate work from selecting the feasible sprint plan. Clear priorities and requirements support the team's planning, but do not erase capacity or the Developers' responsibility for technical work. A useful product contribution gives the team enough understanding to make the selection and discuss its relationship to the goal.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The PM/PO does not dictate how Developers turn selected backlog items into working product increments.

coverage.learning_objective: Understand the PM/PO's role in a Daily Scrum: listening for blockers and scope risk without turning it into a status meeting.

required_facts.statement: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute Developer event to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the upcoming plan.
A Product Owner participates as a Developer when actively working on sprint backlog items; it is not inherently a management status meeting.
Identify impediments or unresolved product questions from the discussion and clarify who needs to act on them.
Handle detailed follow-up outside the short event and involve the appropriate owner instead of interrupting team self-management.

teaching_blocks.title: Daily Standup (PM/PO Involvement) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: During a Daily Scrum, someone reports that unfinished-status information is blocking selected work. A PM may need to help clarify the product question, but turning the event into a long management update would change its purpose. The event inspects Developer progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapts the upcoming plan.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute Developer event to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the upcoming plan. A Product Owner participates as a Developer when actively working on sprint backlog items; it is not inherently a management status meeting.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify impediments or unresolved product questions from the discussion and clarify who needs to act on them. Handle detailed follow-up outside the short event and involve the appropriate owner instead of interrupting team self-management.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an illustrative 15-minute event, Developers identify that a status definition remains unresolved. Clarify who needs to act, then arrange a detailed follow-up with the appropriate owner outside the short event. Do not require each Developer to report personal productivity to the PM or interrupt team self-management with an extended requirements debate. A Product Owner participates as a Developer when actively working on sprint backlog items; the event is not inherently a management status meeting. The relevant product follow-up in this example is to resolve the question that impedes work toward the Sprint Goal, not to take control of the Developers' plan.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the impediment visible and the response proportionate to the event's purpose. Identifying a product question and its owner does not require solving every detail inside the 15 minutes. The distinction lets the team inspect and adapt its work while ensuring that a necessary clarification is handled by the right people afterward.

segments.label: A 15-minute check on Sprint Goal progress and impediments
segments.summary: The Daily Scrum, also called a daily standup, gives Developers 15 minutes to coordinate their work and plan the next 24 hours. It takes place at the same time and place each day. One typical approach is to discuss how yesterday’s work and today’s planned work support the Sprint Goal, and identify impediments that could prevent progress. Teams may also consider remaining work and adjust their plan when the Sprint Goal is at risk.

teaching_blocks.title: Sprint Review (PM/PO Involvement) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: At the end of a sprint, stakeholders need to inspect completed product work and discuss what should happen next. A Sprint Review is not just a list of tasks marked finished. It connects what was and was not completed to the goal and product direction, then uses feedback to reconsider upcoming priorities.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A sprint review inspects completed product work with stakeholders and gathers feedback about next steps. The review considers completed and incomplete work in relation to the sprint goal and product direction.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Prepare a review agenda with the goal, demonstrations of completed work, stakeholder questions, and feedback capture. Use feedback and changed circumstances to reconsider upcoming priorities and clarify next steps.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative review, begin with the Sprint Goal of making unfinished paid orders visible. Demonstrate the completed summary behavior, explain that detail access remains incomplete if that is the actual state, and invite stakeholder questions about the value and next steps. Capture feedback, such as a concern about which orders belong in the result, alongside changed circumstances relevant to priorities. Use it to clarify upcoming work rather than assuming the old plan must remain untouched. Keep discussion grounded in the completed work and direction. Examining how the team worked belongs to the retrospective, which is distinct from this inspection of product work with stakeholders.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Prepare the goal, demonstrations, questions, and feedback capture as a coherent review agenda. A demonstration without context may leave stakeholders unsure what result to assess. Feedback without a next-step discussion may remain an unused note. The review should help clarify the product's next direction without misrepresenting incomplete work as completed.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A sprint review is distinct from a retrospective, which examines the team’s working process.

required_facts.statement: A sprint retrospective inspects how the team worked and plans improvements to quality and effectiveness.
The Scrum Team examines interactions, processes, tools, problems, and assumptions and chooses useful improvements.
Triage actions about product goals, backlog clarity, or backlog ordering to the Product Owner’s accountability.
Leave technical work planning with Developers and process improvements as collaborative team work rather than automatically assigning every action to the PM/PO.

required_facts.statement: Assign clear follow-up ownership for the chosen improvements and address high-impact changes promptly.

teaching_blocks.title: Sprint Retrospective (PM/PO Involvement) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A retrospective identifies unclear backlog items, a difficult technical handoff, and a recurring team communication problem. The PM cannot simply accept ownership of every action. The event examines how the Scrum Team worked and chooses improvements with ownership appropriate to the issue.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A sprint retrospective inspects how the team worked and plans improvements to quality and effectiveness. The Scrum Team examines interactions, processes, tools, problems, and assumptions and chooses useful improvements.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Triage actions about product goals, backlog clarity, or backlog ordering to the Product Owner’s accountability. Leave technical work planning with Developers and process improvements as collaborative team work rather than automatically assigning every action to the PM/PO. Assign clear follow-up ownership for the chosen improvements and address high-impact changes promptly.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an illustrative retrospective, connect an action to clarify product goals and backlog ordering with the Product Owner's accountability. Leave technical work planning with Developers. Treat the communication-process improvement as collaborative team work and agree a clear follow-up owner rather than automatically assigning it to the PM or PO. Discuss interactions, processes, tools, problems, and assumptions to identify useful improvements. Choose high-impact changes for prompt attention and record who will follow through. If the issue is that requirements were repeatedly unclear, describe that process problem and its improvement, rather than using the retrospective only to review the product demonstration again.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: For each action, ask what kind of improvement it is and who is responsible for the corresponding work. Clear ownership does not mean that one role owns every issue discussed. The retrospective's focus is quality and effectiveness of the team's working process, with selected improvements that can be acted on, not merely a collection of complaints without follow-up.

media.group_title: Inspect team working practices and choose useful improvements

segments.label: A collaborative retrospective: observations, causes, and improvements
segments.summary: A five-step retrospective starts by establishing a collaborative, non-blaming environment. Team members then record positives, things they want to change, and insights, grouping related observations together. The team selects one to three themes and investigates their causes, such as why collaboration is working well or why a shared development server is unreliable. It then agrees improvements: changes to working agreements or work added to the backlog. The presenter groups suggestions into two buckets: working-agreement decisions and backlog actions. Choosing only one or two improvements keeps the next iteration manageable. The retrospective closes by reflecting on how the session could improve, with an optional appreciation round if one has not already happened.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the clip moves from individual observations to shared improvements without blame. The creator calls things to change “deltas”; here, they are improvement opportunities. The presenter groups suggestions into working-agreement decisions and backlog actions; treat this as a facilitation convention, not a universal requirement.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains collaborative inspection and improvement selection, but not PM/PO-versus-Developer ownership, clear follow-up owners, or prompt handling of high-impact changes. The text supplies those responsibilities.

practice_anchor.objective: Triage retrospective actions about unclear product goals, unclear backlog items, backlog ordering, technical work planning, and recurring team communication into 'PM/PO owns' or 'team owns'. Treat 'team owns' as Developers for technical work planning and collaborative team ownership for process improvements.

coverage.learning_objective: Prepare upcoming backlog items (clarify, size, split) so they're ready for a future sprint.

required_facts.statement: Backlog refinement is ongoing review and clarification of upcoming work so the team can plan and execute it.
Refinement can include clarifying requirements, splitting large items, estimating effort, and reconsidering order.
Review an item for a clear user outcome, understood scope, acceptance conditions, dependencies, and manageable size.
Work with the team to resolve gaps, split oversized items, and update estimates and ordering as appropriate.

misconceptions.statement: Refinement is not limited to a single mandatory meeting held once before execution.

teaching_blocks.title: Backlog Refinement in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Upcoming work says “improve the closing summary,” but the team cannot tell its user outcome, scope, or acceptance conditions. Refinement makes that work clearer and more manageable over time. It may involve several kinds of review rather than one mandatory meeting immediately before execution.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Backlog refinement is ongoing review and clarification of upcoming work so the team can plan and execute it. Refinement can include clarifying requirements, splitting large items, estimating effort, and reconsidering order.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Review an item for a clear user outcome, understood scope, acceptance conditions, dependencies, and manageable size. Work with the team to resolve gaps, split oversized items, and update estimates and ordering as appropriate.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative item, clarify whether the intended outcome is finding unfinished orders or opening their details. Review included scope, acceptance conditions, dependencies, and size with the team. If both outcomes create an oversized item, split it into smaller understandable work where appropriate. Resolve missing status definitions, revisit the estimate after clarification, and reconsider the order against current needs. The result is updated upcoming work the team can better understand and plan. Do not preserve an old estimate when it rests on an assumption the review has just changed, or call an item refined solely because its title has been rewritten neatly.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Refinement checks the substance of the item: what value it serves, what behavior it includes, what conditions matter, and what could prevent it from progressing. Those questions help expose gaps before the work is selected. Keep the process ongoing as understanding evolves rather than treating one scheduled discussion as the only possible time to clarify upcoming work.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Refinement is not limited to a single mandatory meeting held once before execution.

media.group_title: Clarifying and sizing upcoming work together

segments.label: A team clarifies, reorders, and splits backlog items
segments.summary: A team regularly refines its backlog and tries shorter, daily sessions instead of longer weekly ones. It starts by establishing a shared understanding of the product goal. Team discussion brings a business risk to light, prompting a change in backlog order, and an irrelevant item is removed. Questions help clarify another item's brief description and acceptance conditions. When team members disagree about whether the item can fit into one sprint, they discuss their assumptions and conclude that it is too large. They split it into smaller items of value, then consider their order and further details. Refinement does not require knowing everything in advance: the team needs enough information to start and a size it is confident it can complete within a sprint.

bridge_note.before: Watch how team questions change an item's details, order, and size. The clip calls acceptance conditions “acceptance criteria”; both refer to the conditions the item must satisfy.
bridge_note.after: The clip demonstrates collaborative clarification and splitting, but not the full readiness checklist or explicit estimate updates. The text covers dependencies, the complete checklist, and revisiting estimates after scope changes.

coverage.learning_objective: Balance technical debt paydown against feature work in prioritization decisions.

required_facts.statement: Technical debt is the future cost or reduced flexibility created by development choices that defer technical work.
Debt can be taken deliberately or arise inadvertently, and its consequences can accumulate over time.
Identify a debt item by describing the deferred work, its current impact, and the likely cost of leaving it unresolved.
Discuss repayment with the team and weigh it against other work using the impact on future delivery and product quality.
Reserve an explicit share of available capacity for debt work when its impact justifies it, and explain the resulting feature-versus-debt tradeoff rather than assuming a universal ratio.

misconceptions.statement: Technical debt is not inherently a bad decision; some tradeoffs can be reasonable under real constraints.

teaching_blocks.title: Technical Debt Management in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Engineering explains that a shortcut in status handling now makes related changes harder. The team must compare addressing that deferred work with delivering new features. Technical debt management makes the current impact and likely future cost visible, instead of dismissing all debt as bad or reserving a universal capacity percentage without justification.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Technical debt is the future cost or reduced flexibility created by development choices that defer technical work. Debt can be taken deliberately or arise inadvertently, and its consequences can accumulate over time.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify a debt item by describing the deferred work, its current impact, and the likely cost of leaving it unresolved. Discuss repayment with the team and weigh it against other work using the impact on future delivery and product quality. Reserve an explicit share of available capacity for debt work when its impact justifies it, and explain the resulting feature-versus-debt tradeoff rather than assuming a universal ratio.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented debt item, describe the deferred status-cleanup work, its current effect on changing the closing summary, and the likely cost of leaving it unresolved. Discuss repayment with engineering alongside feature work, considering future delivery and product quality. Suppose the team chooses to reserve 20% of the available capacity for this particular debt because the described impact justifies it. Explain that this reduces capacity for a planned enhancement and name the resulting tradeoff. The 20% is an example decision, not a recommended ratio for every team. The original shortcut may have been a deliberate choice under real constraints or may have arisen inadvertently; either way, inspect its consequences rather than judging only its label.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Debt describes a future cost or reduced flexibility from deferred technical work. Management therefore needs both an account of the debt and a reasoned repayment choice. Do not assume that all feature work must stop whenever debt exists, or that debt can always be ignored. Make the impact, competing work, and accepted capacity tradeoff explicit for this decision.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Technical debt is not inherently a bad decision; some tradeoffs can be reasonable under real constraints.

segments.label: Technical debt: why deferred work makes future changes harder
segments.summary: Technical debt creates future rework when a quick or limited solution leaves technical work unresolved. Its consequences can accumulate, making subsequent changes harder. The financial-debt analogy illustrates the extreme: maintaining and repairing existing software can consume more effort than delivering new features. This explains why deferred work matters to future delivery, without making every shortcut an unreasonable choice.

teaching_blocks.title: Dependency Tracking (Sprint-Level Blockers) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Selected sprint work cannot progress because another team has not supplied the required status output. At this level, the dependency is a blocker to work toward the Sprint Goal. Tracking it means making the needed output, provider, blocked item, and agreed action visible until the problem is resolved.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A sprint-level blocker is a dependency that prevents selected work from progressing toward the Sprint Goal. Identify the needed output, its provider, the blocked item, and the handoff date.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Confirm the provider’s status and coordinate a workaround, alternative sequence, or escalation with the involved teams. Keep the blocker and agreed action visible until the dependency is resolved.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Create an illustrative blocker record naming the status output, the provider team, the closing-summary item that needs it, and the required handoff date. Confirm the provider's actual status. With the teams involved, consider a workaround, a feasible alternative sequence, or escalation when appropriate. Record the agreed next action and keep the blocker visible while the dependency remains unresolved. If the team can work on an independent part first, that is an alternative sequence to coordinate, not proof that the original dependency has disappeared. Update the record when the needed output is available and the blocker is resolved rather than removing it simply because someone has acknowledged the message.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: A blocker description should let a reader connect what is missing to the selected work it prevents. “Waiting on another team” is less informative than the specific output, provider, item, and handoff. Visibility and coordination support the response; they do not substitute for confirming that the required dependency has actually been met.

video_need.reason: A blocker diagram with status changes would show how the missing output, provider, blocked item, and resolution connect.

practice_anchor.objective: In a sample sprint backlog, flag the closing-summary item blocked by a missing status output from the provider team. practice_anchor.success: The blocking dependency is correctly flagged and linked to work toward the Sprint Goal. Its record identifies the needed output, provider, blocked item, and handoff date, reflects the provider's confirmed status, and proposes a feasible coordinated response. The blocker and next action remain visible until the required output is available; acknowledgment or work on an independent part is not treated as resolution.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make visible the sample sprint backlog and its blocker record: the closing-summary item, missing status output, provider team, handoff date, confirmed provider status, agreed next action, and unresolved or resolved status.

required_facts.statement: Workflow states describe the stages a work item passes through from entry to completion.

required_facts.statement: Cards represent individual work items and columns make their current stages visible.

required_facts.statement: A WIP limit sets the maximum number of items allowed in a workflow stage.
When a stage reaches its limit, help finish or unblock existing items rather than starting additional work in that stage.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/boards :: What is a kanban board? | Atlassian

source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/wip-limits :: Working with WIP limits for kanban | Atlassian

misconceptions.statement: Higher limits are not automatically better; excess parallel work can lengthen delivery time.

teaching_blocks.title: Kanban Board Management in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A board shows several order-product cards in review and more waiting to enter that stage. Starting additional review work may feel productive, but a work-in-progress limit sets a boundary on how many items the stage allows. Board management focuses on finishing or unblocking existing work when that boundary is reached.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Workflow states describe the stages a work item passes through from entry to completion. Cards represent individual work items and columns make their current stages visible.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A WIP limit sets the maximum number of items allowed in a workflow stage. When a stage reaches its limit, help finish or unblock existing items rather than starting additional work in that stage. Review bottlenecks and adjust limits based on observed flow rather than assuming the initial limits are permanent.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Use an illustrative board with Ready, In progress, Review, and Complete columns. Cards represent individual items. If Review has a WIP limit of two and already contains two cards, help finish or unblock those cards rather than adding a third review item. Moving a card should reflect its actual workflow stage, not merely make the board appear less crowded. Observe where flow repeatedly slows and review the limit based on that evidence. These column names and the limit of two are example choices; the concept does not prescribe them for every team. Raising the limit automatically is not necessarily an improvement, since excess parallel work can lengthen delivery time.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read the board as a visible representation of current work state. The columns describe stages; the cards identify items; the limit constrains the number allowed in a stage. A full column invites attention to existing work and bottlenecks, not a reflex to start more in the same stage. Limits can be adjusted after reviewing observed flow rather than assumed permanent from the first setup.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Higher limits are not automatically better; excess parallel work can lengthen delivery time.

video_need.reason: Moving cards on a board would show workflow state, a full WIP-limited stage, and finishing or unblocking work instead of starting more.

media.group_title: Make workflow visible and manage work in progress

segments.label: Represent work with cards and workflow columns
segments.summary: A basic Trello board uses To do, Doing, and Done columns to represent workflow stages. Cards identify work items such as creating a home page or a profile page. Moving a card into Doing indicates that work has started; moving completed work into Done reflects its changed state. The example also distinguishes a completed portion of work from a separate item needed to finish remaining work.

segments.label: Limit work in progress and focus on finishing
segments.summary: A work-in-progress (WIP) limit restricts how many items are underway so the team focuses on finishing current work before starting more. Limits can be set for individual workflow stages. The speaker suggests staffing-based starting limits while acknowledging that no single approach fits every team. Separating waiting items from active work and monitoring both helps reveal bottlenecks and where assistance or resources may be needed.

bridge_note.before: In the first clip, follow cards through workflow columns. In the second, focus on finishing existing work under WIP limits; its staffing-based numbers are starting suggestions, not universal rules.
bridge_note.after: The first clip does not teach WIP limits; the text covers them and the response to a full stage. Neither clip explains revising limits from observed flow; the text supplies that guidance.

source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/definition-of-done :: What is the Definition of Done (DoD) in Agile? | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Create the definition collaboratively with the people responsible for delivering and using the work.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/definition-of-done :: Work with the right team members

required_facts.statement: Apply the shared checklist to an increment before treating it as complete, and resolve any unmet conditions.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/definition-of-done :: What is the Definition of Done (DoD) in Agile? | Atlassian

teaching_blocks.title: Definition of Done in product work
teaching_blocks.content: One person calls an increment complete because its main behavior works; another says agreed quality checks remain unfinished. A shared Definition of Done makes the conditions for considering work complete explicit. It is broader than the acceptance conditions describing one particular item's required behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Definition of Done is the team’s shared set of conditions for considering work complete and ready for customers. The conditions should be specific enough for the team to check completion and quality consistently.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Create the definition collaboratively with the people responsible for delivering and using the work. Apply the shared checklist to an increment before treating it as complete, and resolve any unmet conditions.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented team, collaboratively agree a completion checklist with the people responsible for delivering and using the work. Suppose the agreed conditions include checking intended behavior, completing required quality review, and preparing the stipulated customer-facing information. Apply those actual conditions to the increment. If the summary's item-specific criteria are met but the agreed quality review is not, resolve the unmet shared condition before treating the increment as complete. These sample conditions illustrate a team's agreement, not a universal checklist imposed on every product. A specific criterion such as “completed orders do not appear” still belongs to the particular item and is not identical to the whole shared completion definition.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Ask two distinct questions: did this item deliver its required behavior, and did the increment satisfy the team's shared completion conditions? A clear Definition of Done lets people check the latter consistently. Keep conditions specific enough to verify and resolve missing ones rather than changing the meaning of complete depending on who is reporting progress.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Definition of Done is not identical to the item-specific conditions that describe whether a particular requirement was implemented correctly.

video_need.reason: The shared-completion versus item-specific distinction is clear from the written checklist comparison.

practice_anchor.objective: Check a sample story reported as completed against the team's given Definition of Done checklist and flag missing items.
practice_anchor.success: Flags the required quality review as unmet while recognizing that intended behavior and stipulated customer-facing information have been checked. Identifies that the unmet shared condition must be resolved before treating the work as complete, even though the story's item-specific criteria are met.

misconceptions.statement: Technical availability and a market-facing launch are distinct and need not be the same event.

teaching_blocks.title: Release Management in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The closing-summary work is technically available, but customer-facing preparation and monitoring still need coordination. Release management links goals and scope to timing, responsibilities, dependencies, and readiness work, while including support for problems that appear after release.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Release management coordinates the tactical and strategic steps involved in preparing a product for launch. Release planning connects agreed scope to delivery timing and responsibilities.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Prepare the plan by defining release goals and scope, sequencing work, and identifying dependencies and readiness tasks. Include post-release monitoring and support so unexpected user problems can be identified and addressed.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative release plan, define the selected summary scope and goal, sequence enabling status work before dependent behavior, and identify owners for delivery and readiness tasks. Include the necessary customer-support preparation and post-release monitoring with clear responsibilities. If unexpected user problems appear, the plan should identify how they can be noticed and addressed. Do not assume that making the software technically available is automatically the same event as a market-facing launch. In this example, availability could precede broader customer introduction while preparation is completed. Those events need coordination, but need not be identical in timing or purpose.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read the plan from preparation through post-release response. Scope without timing and ownership leaves coordination unclear; delivery timing without readiness and support overlooks part of the release work. Keep the plan focused on the tactical and strategic steps needed for introduction rather than stopping the explanation at “the code is available.”

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Technical availability and a market-facing launch are distinct and need not be the same event.

required_facts.statement: A North Star metric captures a central measure of the value customers receive from a product.

required_facts.statement: A useful North Star metric reflects customer value, is within the team’s influence, and is connected to sustained business results.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/product-north-star-metric :: Every Product Needs a North Star Metric: Here’s How to Find Yours

required_facts.statement: Choose a candidate by identifying the product’s core customer value and the observable behavior that indicates receipt of that value.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/product-north-star-metric :: Every Product Needs a North Star Metric: Here’s How to Find Yours

required_facts.statement: Identify contributing input metrics that teams can act on to improve the central value measure.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/product-north-star-metric :: Every Product Needs a North Star Metric: Here’s How to Find Yours

misconceptions.statement: Revenue alone may not represent whether customers are receiving the product’s core value.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/product-north-star-metric :: Every Product Needs a North Star Metric: Here’s How to Find Yours

teaching_blocks.title: North Star Metrics in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The shop-order product has many dashboard counts, but the team wants a central measure of customer value. A North Star candidate should reflect what customers receive from using the product, remain within the team's influence, and connect to sustained business results rather than simply being the easiest number to display.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A North Star metric captures a central measure of the value customers receive from a product. A useful North Star metric reflects customer value, is within the team’s influence, and is connected to sustained business results.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Choose a candidate by identifying the product’s core customer value and the observable behavior that indicates receipt of that value. Identify contributing input metrics that teams can act on to improve the central value measure.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the example product's core value is helping shops complete their order work reliably. Consider “shops completing their weekly order review” as a candidate observable behavior indicating receipt of that value. Examine whether it actually reflects the stated value, whether the team can influence it, and how it connects to sustained business results. Identify contributing inputs the team can act on, such as reaching the review and completing it, if those fit the chosen definition. A revenue total may be relevant to the business, but revenue alone may not represent whether customers receive this core value. The candidate requires judgment against those conditions; this example does not establish it as the right North Star for every order product.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Start with the value, then choose the behavior that could indicate customers are receiving it. Do not reverse the process by selecting a convenient count and declaring it central. Contributing input metrics should help teams act on the central measure while preserving the distinction between customer value and an unrelated increase in activity.

teaching_blocks.title: Objectives and Key Results (OKRs) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A team promises to ship a summary, write documentation, and hold a meeting, then calls the list an OKR. Those are activities, but an OKR pairs a desired direction with measured results. The key results should make achievement of the objective assessable rather than just record that work was done.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: An OKR pairs an objective describing a desired direction with key results that measure its achievement. The objective is qualitative and motivating; key results are measurable outcomes with clear targets.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write an OKR by stating the intended improvement and a small set of measurable results that would demonstrate it. Review progress against the key-result targets during the agreed planning period.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented OKR, write the objective “Make closing-time order work more reliable for shop owners.” Pair it with a small set of measurable outcomes, such as increasing weekly review completion from 40% to 50% and reducing the defined rate of overlooked unfinished orders from 10% to 5% during the agreed quarter. These are illustrative targets, not product performance claims. Review progress against them during that planning period. Delivering the summary may be an activity intended to contribute, but completing it does not by itself demonstrate that either key result was achieved. Keep the qualitative objective and quantitative outcome targets distinct.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read each proposed key result and ask whether it measures achievement or merely names something the team will do. The objective communicates direction; the key results define observable success. If the team finishes every activity while the outcome measures remain unchanged, the activity list alone cannot establish that the OKR was achieved.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Completing a list of activities does not by itself demonstrate achievement of a key result.

video_need.reason: The objective, measured key results, and activity contrast fit a static annotated example.

teaching_blocks.title: Leading and Lagging Indicators in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team wants early signals it can act on and later measures showing whether the intended outcome followed. Leading and lagging labels depend on the target outcome being considered. A metric is classified by its relationship to that outcome, not solely by whether its chart appears early in a dashboard.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A leading indicator tracks a precursor that can help predict a later outcome. A lagging indicator measures an outcome after it has occurred.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Classify a metric by asking whether it measures an input or precursor to the target outcome or the realized outcome itself. Use leading indicators to guide timely action and lagging indicators to check whether the intended result followed.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative target of completing a closing review, opening the review may be a precursor and thus a leading candidate, while completed reviews measure the realized outcome and are lagging relative to that target. If the target becomes sustained weekly use, a completed first review could itself be an earlier precursor. State the target each time you classify the metric. Use the precursor to guide timely investigation or action, then inspect the realized outcome to see whether the intended result followed. More openings do not guarantee more completions; a leading indicator can help predict an outcome without making it inevitable.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Ask whether the measure records an input or precursor to the specified outcome, or the outcome after it occurs. Then explain how the team will use each. The distinction helps connect early action to later checking, but does not establish a causal relationship or guarantee from the label alone.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A leading indicator is not a guarantee of the later outcome.

required_facts.statement: A hypothesis states an expectation that can be evaluated using evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Hypothesis Testing in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team expects clearer status labels to improve closing reviews, but “users will love it” is too vague to test. A product hypothesis specifies a change, audience, expected metric direction, and conditions under which the expectation could succeed or be contradicted by evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A hypothesis states an expectation that can be evaluated using evidence. A testable product hypothesis links a specific proposed change to an expected outcome for a defined audience.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write the hypothesis by specifying the change, expected metric direction, affected audience, and conditions for judging the result. Check that the expectation can be contradicted by an observable result rather than merely expressing an aspiration. Set the smallest result that would count as success and identify evidence that would contradict the expectation before testing it.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented hypothesis, write: “For eligible shop owners using the closing summary, clearer status labels will increase weekly review completion by at least 5 percentage points during the planned observation period.” Specify the baseline and the agreed measurement conditions before testing. Define the smallest result that counts as success and what evidence would contradict the expectation, such as no increase or a decrease under those conditions. If the result is a smaller increase, it does not meet the example's specified 5-point success boundary. The hypothesis is an expectation to evaluate, not a statement that the labels already produce that effect or a requirement to reinterpret every favorable result as success.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Make the expectation specific enough that an observable outcome can challenge it. The audience and conditions keep the comparison meaningful, while the success boundary prevents the team from selecting a new definition of success after seeing the result. An aspiration without a possible contradictory observation is not yet a testable product hypothesis.

video_need.reason: An annotated hypothesis revision would help make audience, metric direction, success boundary, and contradictory evidence explicit.

media.group_title: Turn a product hunch into a testable hypothesis

segments.label: Specify a product hypothesis and challenge its assumptions
segments.summary: A product hypothesis makes an expectation specific enough to evaluate with evidence. Start with a defined audience and its problem, describe the current alternative and proposed offering, and state an observable success measure. An illustrative lemonade business expects to sell 500 drinks per day to families visiting a beach on summer weekends. Its assumptions can be challenged separately: interviews can investigate the audience and need, observation can reveal competing refreshments, and a small selling trial can explore the offering. Checking whether enough potential customers visit the beach also challenges the sales expectation. Specificity makes these assumptions testable; it does not establish that they are true.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the example turns a hunch into specific assumptions that evidence can challenge. The creator calls this a “lean” or “venture” hypothesis; here, we use product hypothesis.
bridge_note.after: The clip demonstrates specificity and testability, but not metric direction against a baseline or a precommitted minimum success boundary. The text adds these, judging conditions, and contradictory evidence defined before testing.

practice_anchor.objective: Submit two written hypotheses that replace the vague assumptions “shop owners will love clearer status labels” and “clearer status labels will improve closing reviews.” For each, specify the proposed change, eligible shop-owner audience, expected direction of weekly review completion, baseline, observation period, judging conditions, minimum success result, and an observable result that would contradict the expectation. Use illustrative values rather than collecting real results.
practice_anchor.success: Both hypotheses can be evaluated from the stated evidence and conditions. Each sets a minimum success boundary before testing, identifies contradictory evidence, and distinguishes a favorable result below the boundary from a passing result.

teaching_blocks.title: Analytics Dashboard Interpretation in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A dashboard shows closing reviews rising sharply this week. The team immediately attributes the change to a new summary. Dashboard interpretation first establishes what the metric and chart actually show, then separates that observation from possible explanations requiring further evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A product analytics dashboard brings together measures that support monitoring product performance. Interpret a chart in the context of its metric definition, time window, audience, and benchmark or target.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Look for changes in trend or unusual values and compare related measures before drawing a conclusion. State the observed anomaly separately from a plausible explanation and identify what further evidence would test that explanation.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an illustrative dashboard, completed reviews rise from 400 to 600 in a week, while eligible active shops also rise from 800 to 1,200. The completion proportion remains 50% in both periods. Review the metric definitions, time windows, audience, and benchmark before concluding that owners are completing reviews at a higher rate. State the observed increase in counts separately from an explanation such as newly acquired users or a product change. Identify further evidence that would test the proposed explanation. The supplied arithmetic describes these invented counts; it does not establish why the population grew or why individual customers behaved as they did.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Related measures can change how an apparent anomaly is interpreted. A rise in a total and a rise in the proportion achieving an outcome are different observations. Keep the chart reading precise, and keep explanations labeled as explanations to investigate. A dashboard correlation alone does not establish the cause of a change.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A dashboard correlation alone does not establish why a metric changed.

teaching_blocks.title: Measurement Plan Definition in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team wants to assess whether shop owners complete closing reviews, but has not agreed what data records completion. A measurement plan begins with the product question and defines the key events and contextual properties needed to answer it consistently.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: An event records a user action or occurrence in a product, and event properties describe its context. A tracking plan defines the events and properties to collect so product questions can be answered consistently.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Start a tracking plan with the questions to answer, then list only the key events needed to answer them. For each event, specify its name, when it occurs, source, owner, and relevant properties with types and expected values. Use consistent naming and review the plan with implementation partners before collecting the data.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative tracking plan, start with “How many eligible owners complete a closing review?” Define an event named Closing Review Completed that occurs when the stipulated completion action happens. In this proposed plan, set the source as the closing-summary completion action and the owner as the product analytics partner. Define review date as text in YYYY-MM-DD form, for example 2026-04-08. If shop category is needed for the question, define it as text with the stipulated values “single-owner” and “shift-team.” These names and values are proposed example definitions, not existing tool behavior. Use consistent naming and review the plan with implementation partners before collection. If opening the review is needed to answer a related question, define that separately rather than silently treating an opening as a completion.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: The event says what happened; its properties describe relevant context. The plan connects those records to the questions they should answer and makes timing, source, ownership, and expected values explicit. Tracking every click is not automatically better: it can add unnecessary data and implementation work without improving understanding of the intended product question.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Tracking every click can create unnecessary data and implementation work rather than better understanding.

It specifies the closing-summary completion action as the source and the product analytics partner as the owner. It defines review date as text in YYYY-MM-DD form and includes shop category, with its stipulated text values, only if needed for the stated question. Names are consistent, unnecessary click tracking is excluded, and a review with implementation partners is recorded before collection.

coverage.learning_objective: Analyze a multi-step conversion funnel to find where users drop off.

required_facts.statement: A funnel is an ordered sequence of actions leading toward a target outcome.
Conversion is completion of the target step; drop-off is the loss of users between steps.
Define the steps and timeframe, then compare the number of users reaching each step.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://amplitude.com/docs/analytics/charts/funnel-analysis/funnel-analysis-interpret :: Interpret your Funnel Analysis chart; Set your time options

required_facts.statement: Calculate a step’s conversion as users reaching the next step divided by users at the previous step, and use the difference to locate drop-off.
Investigate the stages with substantial drop-off to identify friction rather than assuming the counts explain its cause.

teaching_blocks.title: Funnel Analysis in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A team knows that some owners begin a closing review but fewer finish it. Funnel analysis locates where the loss occurs by defining an ordered sequence and comparing counts between steps. Those counts help identify stages to investigate, but do not by themselves explain the users' reasons.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A funnel is an ordered sequence of actions leading toward a target outcome. Conversion is completion of the target step; drop-off is the loss of users between steps.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define the steps and timeframe, then compare the number of users reaching each step. Calculate a step’s conversion as users reaching the next step divided by users at the previous step, and use the difference to locate drop-off. Investigate the stages with substantial drop-off to identify friction rather than assuming the counts explain its cause.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Use invented counts within a defined one-week window: 1,000 users open the summary, 600 reach the unfinished-order list, and 300 complete the review. Conversion from opening to the list is 600 ÷ 1,000 = 60%; the count drop-off is 400 users. Conversion from the list to completion is 300 ÷ 600 = 50%; the count drop-off is 300 users. Overall completion from the first step is 300 ÷ 1,000 = 30%. State the steps and timeframe alongside these results so the denominators are clear. Investigate the substantial losses at both stages without claiming the counts prove that a particular button, instruction, or design caused them.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: A step conversion uses the previous step's users as its denominator, not the starting population for every calculation. The corresponding count difference locates loss between those steps. Keep step conversion distinct from overall conversion, then use the mapped losses to choose where to investigate friction. A funnel makes the location of drop-off visible while leaving its cause open to further evidence.

video_need.reason: A stepwise funnel with worked denominators would show conversion and drop-off between steps without implying a cause.

media.group_title: Locate the leak, then investigate the friction

segments.label: Locate funnel drop-off without assuming its cause
segments.summary: An illustrative fitness-store funnel moves from 10,000 ad clicks to 6,000 product-page visitors, 2,500 users adding items to cart, 1,200 starting checkout, and 1,000 purchases. The largest proportional loss occurs between product viewing and adding to cart: 3,500 users leave, about 58.3% of product-page visitors. The largest absolute loss is earlier, from ad clicks to product views: 4,000 users. These counts locate the loss but do not explain it. Observations of browsing behavior suggest overlooked product descriptions and concerns about shipping costs. The store revises its descriptions and introduces free shipping above $50. The example reports product-to-cart conversion reaching 56% and purchases increasing by 18% after a month; these reported improvements do not establish which change caused them.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the funnel locates loss before investigating its cause. The clip's 'biggest leak' is the largest proportional loss, not the largest count loss: ad clicks to product views loses 4,000 users. Its stated 41% baseline is approximate; 2,500 divided by 6,000 is about 41.7%.
bridge_note.after: The clip distinguishes locating drop-off from explaining it. It does not teach timeframe definition or the step-conversion formula; the text supplies both, including worked denominators and count differences.

practice_anchor.objective: Analyze the one-week closing-review funnel: 1,000 users open the summary, 600 reach the unfinished-order list, and 300 complete the review. Calculate each transition's conversion rate and count loss, then identify the biggest leak by count and by percentage.
practice_anchor.success: Reports 60% conversion and a loss of 400 users from summary to unfinished-order list, then 50% conversion and a loss of 300 users from list to completion. teaching_blocks.title: Cohort Analysis in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The overall number of active shops is stable, but that total may combine returning customers and newly acquired ones. Cohort analysis follows a defined group over time so continued use can be examined without hiding it inside an aggregate customer count.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A cohort is a group of users who share a defined characteristic or behavior. Retention analysis follows whether members of a defined cohort return or remain active over time.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define the cohort entry condition and the action that counts as a return, then observe later periods relative to entry. Compare retention across cohorts or periods to see whether continued use is improving or declining.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Define an illustrative cohort as shops completing their first closing review in week A, and define return as completing another review in a later relative week. Suppose 100 shops enter that cohort and 40 complete a review in the first week after entry. Its week-one retention is 40% under that definition. A second cohort entering in week B has 100 shops, with 50 returning in its first week after entry, giving 50%. Compare the same relative period and return action for both. These invented values show a difference in continued use; they do not establish why the cohorts differ. Do not compare the newer cohort's first week with the older cohort's fourth week as if the elapsed periods were equivalent.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Make entry condition, return action, and time since entry explicit. A cohort is defined by a shared characteristic or behavior, not merely any collection of users selected after seeing a favorable result. Following the group through later periods helps distinguish continued use from changes in acquisition that an overall active count can obscure.

teaching_blocks.title: A/B Testing in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A changed closing-summary version has a higher completion rate than the current version, but a favorable difference alone does not establish improvement. A/B testing compares control and changed experiences under planned conditions, using random assignment and a predefined outcome rather than an informal comparison of whichever users received each version.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A/B testing compares a control experience with a changed version to assess a predefined outcome. Random assignment helps make the comparison less dependent on preexisting differences between user groups.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define a hypothesis, primary metric, target audience, and planned run conditions before exposing users to the variants. Treat a favorable metric difference as evidence of improvement only when the reported result is statistically significant under the experiment’s chosen threshold—meaning the reported difference meets a preselected statistical standard for distinguishing an effect from random variation; a Not Significant or Inconclusive result does not establish improvement. Duration feasibility depends on available traffic, baseline performance, and the smallest effect the test is intended to detect. Use those inputs to estimate sample needs and duration before building or starting the experiment.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative experiment, define the hypothesis that clearer status wording improves review completion among eligible shop owners. Specify the primary metric, audience, assignment, and planned run conditions before exposure. Suppose the reported control result is 40% and the changed version is 43%. If the experiment reports Not Significant or Inconclusive under its chosen threshold, that favorable numerical difference does not establish improvement. If the result is statistically significant under that threshold, the favorable difference can be treated as evidence of improvement. These outcomes are illustrative report interpretations, not a significance calculation from the percentages alone. Before building or starting the experiment, use traffic, baseline performance, and the smallest effect to detect to estimate sample needs and duration.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Random assignment helps reduce dependence on preexisting group differences, while the planned metric and conditions define what the comparison is meant to assess. Duration feasibility is not a universal number of days: small desired improvements can need more traffic and longer runtimes than larger effects. Keep this PM-level explanation focused on interpreting the reported outcome and planning inputs rather than inventing a statistical formula or claiming that any favorable difference proves success.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Small desired improvements can require more traffic and longer runtimes than larger effects.

teaching_blocks.title: Data-Driven Decision Making in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Evidence suggests one option, but the team also faces customer context and product constraints not captured in the available historical data. Data-informed and data-driven approaches differ in how strongly data determines the choice. In either discussion, explain what the evidence supports and which assumptions or uncertainties shape the recommendation.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Data-informed decision making uses evidence as an input while also considering context and judgment. Data-driven decision making places stronger emphasis on allowing data to determine the choice.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify the decision and relevant evidence, interpret what the data supports, and consider qualitative context and constraints. Explain the chosen action in terms of the evidence, assumptions, and uncertainties that shaped it.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose an invented dashboard shows more completed closing reviews after a change, while interviews describe unresolved confusion among shops coordinating shifts. Identify the decision: whether to expand the current summary or address the shift-handoff need. Examine what the quantitative evidence says about the defined audience and outcome, then consider the qualitative context and constraints. A data-informed recommendation uses evidence as an input alongside that judgment. A more data-driven approach places stronger emphasis on letting data determine the choice. If you recommend the handoff improvement, explain the supporting observations and uncertainty instead of saying the current dashboard proves that new direction will work. Historical data may not capture the opportunity or context of the proposed direction.

teaching_blocks.content: Begin with the decision, not with whichever chart is available. Interpret the relevant evidence, name what remains unknown, and state how context influenced the action. This makes the recommendation inspectable without treating data as either irrelevant or an all-purpose answer to every product question.

teaching_blocks.title: Feature Flags in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team wants to introduce a closing-summary change gradually and retain a way to withdraw it if quality problems appear. A feature flag controls whether specified users receive the feature without requiring a new deployment for every exposure change. The rollout plan still needs audience, checks, and rollback conditions.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A feature flag changes whether specified users receive a feature without requiring a new deployment for each exposure change. Percentage rollout exposes a controlled fraction of eligible users to the feature.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Choose the eligible audience and initial exposure, monitor the result, and expand exposure only after checking readiness. Preserve an explicit rollback option so a problematic change can be turned off or withdrawn. Write explicit exposure stages with a success-metric and feedback check before expanding, and a quality rollback trigger such as errors in the logs that calls for switching the flag off until the problem is fixed.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented staged rollout, define eligible shop owners and begin with 10% exposure. Before expanding to 50% and then 100%, check the agreed completion metric, customer feedback, and readiness at each stage. Record an explicit quality rollback trigger, such as the stipulated error condition appearing in logs, that calls for switching the flag off until the problem is fixed. Those percentages and stages are example choices, not a universal schedule. Preserve the withdrawal option rather than treating expansion as automatic once the calendar advances. If completion improves during exposure, the flag alone does not establish that the change caused the improvement.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Separate deployment from exposure changes, and separate rollout control from causal evidence. The flag lets the team specify who receives the feature and adjust that exposure. Monitoring and readiness checks determine whether the example plan should expand or roll back. Write the stages and triggers explicitly so “gradual rollout” does not hide an undefined sequence or response to problems.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear

teaching_blocks.title: Holdout Groups in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team wants a comparison baseline that remains excluded while a change is observed over time. A holdout is a randomly selected subset kept out of specified changes. Its usefulness depends on a defined audience, comparison metric, observation period, and consistent assignment and exclusions.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A holdout group is a randomly selected subset excluded from a change so it remains a comparison baseline. Comparing target outcomes for exposed users with the held-out baseline helps estimate the change’s incremental effect over time.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define the eligible audience, holdout size, excluded changes, comparison metric, and observation period. Choose the holdout size using both available traffic and the statistical needs of the comparison; Amplitude specifies a configurable range of 1–10%, not a universal requirement. Keep assignment and exclusions consistent through the observation period so baseline users do not receive the treatment.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative eligible audience, select a 5% holdout and keep it excluded from the specified closing-summary change throughout the observation period. Compare the defined completion outcome for exposed users with the held-out baseline to help estimate incremental effect over time. Choose the holdout size using traffic and statistical comparison needs, not just because 5% is convenient. In Amplitude, the configurable range is 1–10%; that tool-specific range is not a universal requirement for every holdout. Also check which experiments were configured to include this holdout. teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example

Keep assignment and exclusions consistent rather than moving users between groups to improve a result. The comparison helps estimate the change's incremental effect; the holdout definition, size, exclusions, metric, and period explain what is actually being compared.

Maintaining that baseline has costs: some users do not receive new features, potentially for months, and teams must coordinate to preserve separate experiences. Holdouts are useful when the value of measuring longer-term effects justifies those costs.

teaching_blocks.title: Launch Readiness Assessment in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The feature appears ready technically, but support preparation or monitoring may still be incomplete. Launch readiness assesses the capabilities needed to introduce and support the product safely. A recommendation should point to evidence and unmet gates, not rely on a general impression that the team has worked hard.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Launch readiness checks whether the capabilities needed to safely introduce and support the product are in place. Readiness includes technical quality, support preparation, sales preparation, monitoring, and operational response.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Complete each readiness check with evidence, a responsible owner, and an unresolved action for any failed item. Use the agreed checklist to recommend proceeding or holding, explicitly identifying any unmet gate and the risk it creates.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative checklist, assess technical quality, support preparation, sales preparation, monitoring, and operational response. Record evidence and a responsible owner for each check. Suppose the technical-quality owner has recorded completion of the agreed checks, but the monitoring owner has not completed the required alert check. Record monitoring as an unmet gate, assign its owner the action of completing and documenting that check, and identify the risk that unexpected user problems might not be noticed promptly. Recommend holding under this example checklist until the gate is met. Conversely, a proceed recommendation should explain how the agreed gates have been met. Do not turn the sample dimensions into a claim that every launch has exactly the same checklist or that a green technical item makes every other readiness dimension irrelevant.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Link the recommendation to the actual agreed checks. Evidence supports the status; the owner and unresolved action explain how a failed item will be addressed; the risk explains why it matters to the launch decision. A checklist filled with unsupported green labels does not give the same basis for a go/no-go recommendation.
